say.text: Two women both have peau d'orange, the orange-peel skin over the breast.
Woman A has a 3 cm lump, and her skin is neither red nor warm. Woman B is red, warm and swollen, with no lump you can feel.
Which one has T4d inflammatory carcinoma?

choices.label: Woman A, the one with a 3 cm lump
Woman B, red, warm and swollen
Both, since the skin signs match
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: T4d names a whole clinical picture, not one sign. Ask how much of the breast is involved, and whether it looks red and warm.
That choice is not right.
A lump with peau d'orange looks like advanced cancer, but peau d'orange is a skin sign, and one skin sign does not make the T4d picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A sign is not the syndrome, so check the whole picture before you assign a T category.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Matching skin signs feel like one disease, but T4d needs the whole inflammatory picture, and a skin sign on its own is only skin involvement.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the picture, not the matching signs.

say.text: Yes. Woman B has the whole inflammatory picture: red, warm and swollen, with peau d'orange over at least a third of the breast.
Peau d'orange on its own is skin involvement, T4b, so Woman A is staged by her skin and size, not as T4d.
Woman B is T4d. Inflammatory carcinoma is a red, warm, swollen breast with peau d'orange over at least a third of it, often with no discrete lump.
Woman A's 3 cm lump with peau d'orange is T4b: skin involvement, not the inflammatory picture.
Extension to the chest wall makes a tumour T4a. Which of these findings is chest-wall involvement?

choices.label: Tumour fixed to pectoralis major alone
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: T4a is the chest wall itself: the ribs, the intercostal muscles and the serratus. Ask which finding reaches those structures, not which one lies on a muscle.
That choice is not right.
Fixity to the pectoralis feels like chest-wall spread because the muscle lies over the chest, but pectoralis major alone is not in the T4a list.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Chest wall means the ribs, intercostals and serratus, so check the list before you count a muscle.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Peau d'orange is a real finding, but it is skin involvement, T4b, and it does not put the tumour on the chest wall.
Yes. Serratus anterior is part of the chest wall, so a tumour that invades it is T4a.
Skin findings are T4b, and pectoralis major alone does not count as chest wall.
The chest wall for T4a is the ribs, the intercostal muscles and the serratus anterior. Invading serratus anterior is therefore T4a.
Fixity to pectoralis major alone is not T4a. Peau d'orange and satellite skin nodules are skin involvement, T4b.
A 4 cm tumour is fixed when the pectoralis is contracted, but the ribs and intercostals move freely.
What is its T category?

choices.label: T4a, because the pectoralis fixes it
T3, because it is over 3 cm
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Size sets the T category first. Then ask whether the ribs, intercostals or serratus are involved; muscle fixity alone is a different question.
That choice is not right.
Fixity to the pectoralis is tested because it looks like chest-wall spread, but the T4a list is the chest wall itself, and pectoralis major alone is not on it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the T4a list before you count fixity.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A tumour is T3 only when it is over 5 cm, and this one is 4 cm.
Yes. A 4 cm tumour is T2 by size, and fixity to pectoralis major does not change that.
Only the chest wall itself, the ribs, intercostals and serratus, makes it T4a.
Size gives T2, since over 2 cm up to 5 cm is T2. Fixity is tested with the muscle contracted, but it does not make the tumour T4a.
Only the chest wall itself makes T4a: ribs, intercostal muscles and serratus anterior.
Patient X has a hard node above the collarbone on the same side as her breast cancer. Patient Y has the same node on the opposite side.
Which patient has M1, distant metastasis?

choices.label: Both, since any node above the collarbone is M1
Patient Y, the node on the opposite side
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check each node on two counts: its height, and which side of the body it sits on. Ask which side current staging treats as distant.
That choice is not right.
Old classifications counted every node above the collarbone as distant, which is why height feels like M1; current staging also looks at which side the node is on.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check the side of the node as well as its height before you call it distant.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Nodes on the same side are nodal, but calling both nodal misses that the side of the node can change the M category.
Yes. A node above the collarbone on the opposite side is distant disease, M1.
The same-side node is still nodal, N3c, and not M1.
Patient Y has M1. Current American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging counts contralateral axillary or supraclavicular nodes as distant.
Patient X's same-side supraclavicular node is N3c. Older PYQs expected M1 for any supraclavicular node, but current staging places same-side nodes on the nodal ladder.
Patient A is 38, with a 1.5 cm early cancer, no symptoms and no palpable nodes.
Patient B has stage III disease and bone pain.
Which patient needs staging scans for distant spread?

choices.label: Both, a bone scan for each patient
Neither, staging waits until after surgery
Patient B, the stage III patient with pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Metastatic scans follow the stage and the symptoms, not the commonest site of spread. Ask which patient has one of those two features.
That choice is not right.
Bone is the commonest site of distant spread, so a bone scan feels routine, but metastatic imaging is for locally advanced disease or symptoms, not for every patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Bone is where cancer goes, but the stage and symptoms decide who needs the scan.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Staging is not postponed for symptoms or locally advanced disease; metastatic imaging is done in those patients.
Yes. Stage III disease, or a symptom such as bone pain, is the indication for metastatic imaging.
Patient A is early and asymptomatic, so she needs local treatment planning, not a routine bone scan.
Metastatic imaging, a CT of chest and abdomen, a bone scan or positron emission tomography CT (PET-CT), is for locally advanced disease or symptoms. Patient B gets it; Patient A does not.
Bone is the commonest site of distant spread, mostly osteolytic. The site does not decide who gets scanned.
Bone is the commonest site of distant spread, followed by lung, liver and brain.
The single most important prognostic factor is axillary lymph node status.
